subsystems.name: Pulse synthesis
subsystems.role: generates the microwave and baseband waveforms that flip qubit states.

subsystems.name: Timing and synchronisation
subsystems.role: keeps every channel phase-locked to one shared reference so pulses across the machine align to picoseconds.
parts: oven-controlled crystal or atomic clock reference

subsystems.name: Readout acquisition
subsystems.role: captures the faint microwave signal reflected from each qubit and extracts its state.

subsystems.name: Real-time control core
subsystems.role: sequences pulses, applies corrections and closes feedback loops without software in the way.
parts: field-programmable gate array or custom ASIC

subsystems.name: Cryogenic signal path
subsystems.role: carries signals from room temperature down to the qubit chip without adding noise.
parts: shielded coaxial lines and twisted pairs

subsystems.name: Cryo-CMOS multiplexers
subsystems.role: operates inside the fridge at a few kelvin so one cable serves many qubits.

subsystems.name: Control software
subsystems.role: turns gate sequences into calibrated waveforms and manages daily recalibration.

buildSteps.title: Specify the signal chain
buildSteps.detail: Set the channel count, bandwidth and noise budget. A transmon qubit near 5 GHz needs pulses tens of nanoseconds long, so each channel must carry hundreds of megahertz of clean instantaneous bandwidth.

buildSteps.title: Design the digital core
buildSteps.detail: Define an FPGA or ASIC containing the pulse sequencer, oscillators, mixers and decimation filters, with enough waveform memory for long experiments.

buildSteps.title: Lay out the radio-frequency board
buildSteps.detail: Route controlled-impedance traces, place converters next to the logic, shield aggressively and manage heat so channels do not drift into each other.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and skew-align
buildSteps.detail: Build the units, then measure and correct the arrival-time difference between channels against a single clock until they agree to picoseconds.

buildSteps.title: Write the control stack
buildSteps.detail: Compile gate sequences into sample-level waveforms, and build calibration routines that find the right amplitudes, frequencies and phases for each qubit.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the hardware
buildSteps.detail: Measure phase noise, spurious tones, harmonic distortion, crosstalk and noise floor across temperature and time, since qubit fidelity tracks directly with these numbers.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate cryo-CMOS versions
buildSteps.detail: Tape out the multiplexer chips at a CMOS foundry, package them for deep-cryogenic operation, and re-characterise at 4 K and below, because transistor thresholds and noise shift markedly when cold.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with the fridge
buildSteps.detail: Wire the controller through attenuators, filters and circulators down the dilution refrigerator stages, then calibrate the whole chain end to end against the qubit chip.

prerequisites.why: microwave-driven qubits set the frequency, bandwidth and fidelity requirements the control hardware must meet.
pulse shaping needs multi-gigabit-per-second DACs and ADCs with enough resolution to keep quantisation noise below qubit error rates.
qubit phase coherence comes straight from the reference oscillator's stability, and channel alignment depends on one shared clock.
both the qubits and any in-fridge control chips need millikelvin and 4 K stages with limited cooling power.
moving multiplexing and memory into the fridge cuts the wiring bottleneck, but cold transistor behaviour is still being mapped.
error-corrected operation needs measurement and feedback within microseconds, faster than general-purpose software allows.

pathway.milestone: room-temperature rack controllers with tens to hundreds of synchronised channels
pathway.unlocks: hands-on control of machines in the hundreds-of-qubits range, with most effort going into calibration.

pathway.milestone: cryo-CMOS multiplexers running at about 4 K, cutting cable count by roughly an order of magnitude
pathway.unlocks: machines with thousands of qubits whose wiring and heat load stay manageable.

pathway.milestone: controllers co-designed and co-packaged with qubit chips, with microsecond-latency feedback loops
pathway.unlocks: error-corrected logical qubits, where decoding happens before the quantum state decays.

pathway.milestone: modular, networked control with optical links into the cryostat and standard interfaces between qubit and control vendors
pathway.unlocks: fault-tolerant machines needing millions of physical qubits, where control cost and power, not qubit count alone, decide feasibility.
